stories.title: Microsoft Offers Exit Packages to a Quarter of Its Workforce
stories.story:
Microsoft has offered voluntary buyouts to roughly 60,000 employees — about 27 percent of its entire global workforce — in what is the company's largest workforce restructuring in its history. The offer targets workers at experience level 70 or below, covering staff up to the vice president rank, in the United States, Canada, India, and the United Kingdom. Employees have until early December to decide; those who accept leave on December 31.

The headline is not the layoffs — it is the math behind them. Microsoft's capital expenditures for the September quarter are expected to surpass $50 billion, up from roughly $35 billion in the same period a year earlier. Azure revenue has crossed $100 billion annually for the first time, and Microsoft 365 Copilot has reached over 30 million paid seats. The company is not shrinking because it is failing. It is shrinking because the kind of growth AI infrastructure demands — data centers, chips, electricity — does not scale through headcount. Human labor is the variable cost being cut to fund fixed capital.

This is the structural story of the AI transition made visible: the same technology a company sells is also the tool it uses to justify needing fewer of the people who used to sell it. Microsoft ran a smaller voluntary retirement program in April; roughly 30 percent of eligible workers took it. If a similar share accepts this round, the company could shed nearly 18,000 people before the new year — all without a single announced layoff. The soft vocabulary of "voluntary exit" masks a hard directional bet: the next era of software is built in server halls, not office parks.
stories.hook: Microsoft isn't laying people off because the business is shrinking — it's laying people off because the business is changing shape entirely.

stories.title: SK Hynix Posts an 80% Profit Margin on AI Memory
stories.story:
For most of its history, making memory chips was a brutal commodity business: prices swung wildly, margins collapsed in downturns, and the only survivors were those who could stomach the cycle. SK Hynix just turned that logic inside out.

On October 28 the South Korean chipmaker reported that third-quarter revenue reached 104.6 trillion won — roughly $73 billion — the first time any quarter in its history has cleared the 100-trillion-won mark. Operating profit came in at 83.3 trillion won, up 632% from a year earlier, yielding an operating margin of 80%. For every dollar of product it shipped, Hynix kept eighty cents before interest and taxes. That is a margin more commonly associated with software monopolies than factories full of silicon wafers.

The mechanism is High Bandwidth Memory, or HBM — stacks of DRAM dies bonded vertically and designed specifically to feed the data-hungry processors inside AI training clusters. Hynix's new HBM4 generation ramped faster than expected, server DDR5 volumes surged, and prices for both rose sharply. The company has now posted record revenue and profit for six consecutive quarters.

What happens next is the more consequential signal. Hynix says it has signed long-term supply contracts with 14 customers, locking in more than half its production capacity through 2027 and 2028, and projects that memory demand will exceed supply through 2030. It is also breaking ground on a Solidigm NAND fab in the United States at an estimated cost of 60 trillion won — the kind of capital commitment that only makes sense if management believes the AI infrastructure buildout is structural, not cyclical.

The risk is that it is. If AI hyperscalers ever pause their spending, margins at these levels compress fast. But for now, a company that once prayed to survive downturns is returning 100 trillion won to shareholders in a single year.
stories.hook: When a chip factory runs an 80% operating margin, you're not really selling hardware anymore — you're selling scarcity.
stories.source: Seoul Economic Daily / SK Hynix Q3 2026 earnings filing

stories.title: Jio Goes Public, Remaking India's Corporate Landscape
stories.story:
For two decades, Reliance Industries kept everything under one roof. On Wednesday morning that changed. Jio Platforms — Mukesh Ambani's telecom and digital services unit — made its debut on the National Stock Exchange, surging 21% from its IPO price of ₹1,119 to open at ₹1,358, pushing its market capitalisation to roughly $131.5 billion. That made it India's second-most valuable listed company, behind only its parent, Reliance itself, and ahead of rival Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank.

The numbers underneath the listing are what make this consequential beyond the ticker tape. The IPO raised $3.2 billion, India's largest ever, and attracted $77 billion in bids — 22 times oversubscribed, with more than 13.8 million individual applicants. Jio serves 530 million telecom customers. Meta and Google are both existing backers. The proceeds are earmarked primarily to retire debt at its telecom subsidiary, a structural deleveraging that gives Jio a cleaner balance sheet as a standalone entity.

The deeper story is strategic. Reliance was built on oil refining and petrochemicals. Ambani has spent years signalling that its future is consumer technology, and this listing is the mechanism that enforces that pivot — giving Jio its own currency, its own shareholders, and its own accountability. A separately listed Jio can raise capital, make acquisitions, and pursue partnerships on its own terms. India, meanwhile, has quietly become the world's busiest IPO market by deal count in 2026, with 246 listings so far. The question now is whether Jio's valuation — already at the upper edge of analyst targets on day one — reflects India's potential or merely its enthusiasm.
stories.hook: When a 530-million-subscriber telecom company needs its own stock listing to escape its parent's shadow, the parent was never really an oil company to begin with.

stories.title: The Fed Holds, But the Word 'December' Does the Work
stories.story:
The Federal Reserve concluded its October meeting today and, as virtually every economist expected, left its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75–4.00 percent. A Reuters survey found 94 of 100 economists anticipated no move. Markets priced a 90 percent chance of a hold. The decision itself was not the story.

The story was what Chair Kevin Warsh said next. The Fed raised rates by 25 basis points in September — its first hike since July 2023 — and the minutes released earlier this month showed that most participants judged another increase "likely appropriate by year end." That means December. And with September CPI running at 3.7 percent year-over-year while the economy added a meager 29,000 jobs last month, Warsh faces a nearly impossible rhetorical task: convincing markets the Fed is neither panicking about inflation nor ignoring it.

The mechanism that makes this consequential is the AI debt machine. Building and filling data centers now requires enormous capital, and companies — even hyperscalers like Meta and Amazon — are increasingly borrowing to fund that expansion. Higher rates make that borrowing more expensive. Broadcom just arranged $63 billion in bank financing to lease chips to Anthropic. When the yield curve tightens, deals like that reprice immediately.

Markets have already priced roughly three more hikes over the next twelve months. If Warsh's press conference today confirms December as a near-certainty, the AI trade — which has been the load-bearing wall of the S&P 500 all year — faces a structural test it has not yet had to pass at these valuations.
stories.hook: The Fed didn't move rates today — it moved December.
stories.source: CNBC, Admiral Markets, EBC Financial Group, CME FedWatch
